newsitem.title: INDIA: India Hindu party could hand Deve Gowda victory.
newsitem.headline: India Hindu party could hand Deve Gowda victory.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda might win a helping hand in a vote of confidence next week from the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which indicated on Wednesday it could abstain from the contest.

The main opposition party opposes Deve Gowda's 15-party United Front coalition, which lost the vital support of the Congress party on Sunday. But politicians said the BJP does not want to help propel Congress into power, either.

"We are not going to support any of the two," BJP spokesman K.L. Sharma told a news conference, referring to the vote of confidence set for April 11 which is widely seen as a contest between Deve Gowda and Congress chief Sitaram Kesri.
BJP politicians said Sharma's comment meant the party might abstain in the vote, ensuring the government would not fall and blocking Congress from taking power.
"The BJP is truly terrified of elections under a Congress government," a leader of the ruling United Front alliance told Reuters.

"Its assessment, a correct one I believe, is that the Congress would win over powerful regional satraps from the United Front as its own electoral allies. The BJP knows that would be disastrous for its own survival."

A senior BJP official said on Tuesday that his party would prefer to face elections, which many analysts believe will come soon irrespective of the outcome of the test vote, under Deve Gowda rather than Kesri.
"We would rather have Deve Gowda as interim prime minister than Kesri," a senior BJP leader said on Tuesday.
Kesri suprised friends and foes on Sunday when he announced that Congress had withdrawn its make-or-break support for Deve Gowda's 10-month-old centre-left coalition.

Congress leaders said Kesri's excellent ties with Defence Minister Mulayam Singh Yadav, a former chief minister of Uttar Pradesh, could prompt the two to forge an alliance in India's most populous state.
Kesri's good standing with Laloo Prasad Yadav, chief minister of the second most populous state of Bihar, was also at the back of the BJP's mind.

"If he gets both these state leaders, given their influence with Moslem voters and lower caste Hindus, it could have a powerful nationwide impact in favour of the Congress," one Kesri aide told Reuters.

Asked if the BJP would abstain in the test vote, a senior official in the rightwing party said: "We could. We can keep Deve Gowda as prime minister, until we decide to face elections under his government rather than Kesri's."
The BJP fears that if Deve Gowda lost the test vote, President Shankar Dayal Sharma would ask Kesri to form a new government.
"By abstaining from the confidence vote, the BJP could give Deve Gowda a new lease of life," political analyst Pran Chopra said in a television interview.
The BJP controls 193 deputies in the 545-seat Lok Sabha, the lower house of parliament. The Congress has the support of 140 and Deve Gowda's coalition commands 180 lawmakers.
The BJP held power for 12 days in May after inconclusive general elections but quit when it was unable to muster enough support to win a vote of confidence.

By Tuesday, Kesri appeared to have realised that his hopes of succeeding Deve Gowda had receded. "I am not against any member of the Steering Committee (of the United Front). My only complaint is against Deve Gowda," he said.
